Baby & Child

Brain tumors in children: symptoms, treatment and recovery

Updated: November 10, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A child’s persistent headache, new balance difficulty or unexplained vomiting deserves attention, but these symptoms do not by themselves mean a brain tumor. Assessment looks at the whole pattern and the child’s examination. If a tumor is found, care depends on its location and biology, the child’s needs and which treatments can help while protecting developing brain function.

Changes that deserve a medical assessment

Brain tumors can affect the nervous system directly or interfere with the movement of cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms may develop gradually or appear suddenly. Repeated headaches, vomiting, altered vision, a new squint, unsteadiness, changes in speech or hearing, and unexplained weakness can all warrant assessment. Many children with these symptoms have other conditions; a symptom list cannot distinguish the cause.

Babies may show feeding difficulties, unusual irritability, poor growth, increasing head size or loss of skills. Older children may have changes in concentration, schoolwork, energy or behavior. Spinal tumors can cause persistent back pain, difficulty walking, altered sensation or changes in bladder and bowel function. Arrange prompt medical review for unexplained, persistent or worsening changes rather than waiting for several signs to occur together.

When to seek urgent or emergency help

Seek urgent medical advice for a child’s headache with vomiting or vision problems, or a headache that worsens, wakes them at night or is worse with coughing or bending. Call emergency services for severe breathing difficulty, inability to wake the child, sudden marked weakness, new difficulty speaking or walking, sudden loss of vision, or an abrupt extremely painful headache. These can indicate several serious conditions, not only tumors.

Call emergency services for a first seizure that is happening now, a seizure lasting longer than usual or more than five minutes when the usual duration is unknown, or repeated seizures without recovery. Follow an existing seizure emergency plan if one has been provided. A first suspected seizure that has stopped still needs urgent medical assessment if the child has not been evaluated. Do not postpone urgent care to arrange a routine scan.

Causes, inherited risk and radiation questions

For most children, no clear cause is found, and there is no ordinary parenting choice to blame. A minority have a condition that increases susceptibility, such as neurofibromatosis type 1, Li–Fraumeni syndrome or tuberous sclerosis complex. These are predisposition conditions, not names for brain tumors. A change found in tumor cells does not automatically mean the child inherited it. The team can explain whether genetic counseling or testing would help the child or family.

Previous radiation treatment to the head can increase later tumor risk. Diagnostic X-rays and CT scans use much lower doses; clinicians should avoid unnecessary exposure and use child-appropriate settings. When CT is needed, its immediate benefit generally outweighs the small future radiation risk. Mobile phones and power lines involve different, non-ionizing exposures: current evidence has not established that they cause childhood brain tumors. Research has limits, so this is not a claim that every possible exposure has been proved risk-free.

The first appointment and referral

The clinician will ask when the changes began, whether they are progressing, and what happens between episodes. Describe vomiting, headaches, vision, movement, seizures and any loss of abilities. Bring information about medicines, previous cancer treatment and known genetic conditions. A short dated account of what you have noticed can help explain the pattern; gathering it should never delay urgent help.

Examination is adapted to the child’s age and may assess eye movements and vision, strength, reflexes, coordination, sensation and alertness. Growth and development also matter. Concerning findings may lead to assessment by a pediatric neurologist, neurosurgeon or neuro-oncology team. There is no routine brain-tumor screening program for all well children. Children with particular genetic risks may instead have a specialist surveillance plan.

What MRI and CT can tell the team

MRI gives detailed images of the brain and sometimes the spine without ionizing radiation. It can show a suspected tumor’s position, size and relationship to nearby structures. Contrast given into a vein may improve the images. Staying still matters, so some children need preparation with a play or child-life specialist, sedation or anesthesia. Tell the imaging team about implants, kidney problems or previous contrast reactions, and follow their eating and drinking instructions.

CT uses X-rays and is quicker, which can be useful when an urgent answer is needed or MRI is unsuitable. A child does not automatically need both tests. Ask what question the scan is meant to answer and how you will receive the result. Imaging may strongly suggest a diagnosis, but deciding what the abnormality means can also require specialist review and, in some cases, tissue testing.

Biopsy, molecular tests and lumbar puncture

A biopsy provides a small piece of tissue for examination, sometimes during an operation that also removes tumor. Testing can identify cell features and molecular changes that affect diagnosis and treatment. It is not a universal requirement: in selected situations, imaging and other findings may be sufficient or taking tissue may pose an unacceptable risk. The neurosurgical team should explain the expected value of a sample and the risks of obtaining it.

A lumbar puncture takes a sample of cerebrospinal fluid from the lower back. It may help assess certain tumors that can spread through that fluid; it is not a routine test for every suspected brain tumor. Clinicians must check that it is safe, particularly when raised pressure inside the skull is possible. A scan alone does not replace this safety assessment. Blood tests may also check organ function and treatment readiness, rather than providing a general blood test that rules brain tumors in or out.

How the treatment plan is chosen

The team combines the diagnosis, molecular findings, tumor position and extent with the child’s age, symptoms and health. A noncancerous tumor can still need treatment if it threatens vision, hormones or vital structures. Conversely, selected stable tumors can be monitored with scheduled examinations and imaging. Observation is an active plan with agreed reasons to reconsider treatment; it is not a decision for families to make from a scan report alone. Grade gives information about tumor behavior, but it must be interpreted alongside the precise tumor type and molecular findings.

Ask what each option aims to achieve: cure, long-term control, protection of a function or relief of symptoms. Discuss expected benefits, immediate risks, possible later effects and whether a suitable clinical trial exists. Parents and children who can participate should have opportunities to ask questions and express priorities. The team can also advise whether a second opinion is feasible without an unsafe delay. Different tumor types require different plans.

Surgery and support around an operation

An operation may remove the tumor, reduce its size, obtain a diagnosis or relieve pressure. Removing every visible part is not always the safest goal: preserving movement, speech, vision and other functions may require leaving tissue in place. Some tumors cannot be removed safely. Surgery can be the main treatment for one child and only one part of treatment for another.

Additional care may include medicines for swelling or seizures and, when fluid drainage is blocked, a procedure to manage hydrocephalus. Not every child needs a shunt. After surgery, the team monitors neurological function and plans further care using the recovery, scans and tissue results. Hospital stay and rehabilitation needs vary; discharge is based on the child’s condition and the support needed at home, not a fixed number of days.

Radiotherapy and the developing brain

Radiotherapy aims energy at the tumor or an area at risk of remaining disease. Treatment planning tries to protect nearby healthy tissue. The balance is especially important in very young children because the brain is still developing. Depending on the diagnosis, chemotherapy or other approaches may delay or avoid radiation, but there is no universal rule that every child under three must never receive it.

Ask the radiation oncologist why radiation is recommended now, which area will be treated and what effects are most relevant to your child. More focused techniques, including proton treatment in selected cases, can reduce exposure to surrounding tissue but do not remove all risk. Tiredness, nausea, skin changes and hair loss in the treated area can occur. Learning, growth, hormone, hearing or vision effects may emerge later and influence follow-up.

Chemotherapy and treatments guided by tumor biology

Chemotherapy uses medicines to control or destroy tumor cells. Treatment may be given into a vein or by mouth in planned courses, alone or with surgery or radiation. Its role is determined by the specific disease and treatment goal, not simply by whether a tumor is described as fast-growing. The team monitors response and may adjust timing or treatment when recovery between courses is needed.

Some tumors have molecular changes that make a targeted medicine an option. A molecular finding does not guarantee that a particular drug will work or is suitable for the child’s age and situation. Ask which result supports the recommendation, what benefit is expected and what monitoring is needed. These treatments can also cause adverse effects. Do not start supplements or alter prescribed cancer medicines without the treating team’s advice.

Managing side effects and knowing whom to call

The side effects of treatment differ between medicines and radiation plans. Nausea, appetite changes, mouth soreness, tiredness, hair loss, diarrhea or other bowel changes can affect everyday life. Some chemotherapy lowers blood-cell counts, increasing infection or bleeding risk. Tell the team about problems early so it can adjust symptom relief, nutrition or other support. Do not assume a new headache or neurological change is simply an expected treatment effect.

Before going home, obtain written instructions and an out-of-hours contact number. Fever or infection during cancer treatment needs immediate advice; in a child with low infection-fighting cells it is a medical emergency. Follow the team’s temperature threshold and measurement instructions, and seek emergency care if you cannot reach them promptly or the child is very unwell. Persistent vomiting, poor fluid intake, unusual bleeding or new symptoms also need prompt contact. Use emergency services for the severe neurological or breathing signs described above.

Watching recovery after discharge

Follow the surgical team’s specific instructions for medicines, wound care, bathing, activity and the next review. Seek urgent help for fever, increasing redness or swelling around the wound, or fluid leaking from the incision. A stiff neck, worsening headache, repeated vomiting or a child becoming generally unwell after neurosurgery also needs urgent assessment. Do not wait until the next scheduled appointment to report these changes.

New weakness, loss of coordination, changed speech or vision, unusual behavior, or a new bladder or bowel problem should be reported promptly. Sudden neurological loss, marked confusion, reduced responsiveness or severe breathing difficulty warrants emergency care. Recovery can fluctuate, but a significant deterioration should not be dismissed as tiredness. The discharge plan should distinguish changes that are expected for this child from those requiring immediate review.

Rehabilitation, communication and school

Recovery involves more than the surgical wound or scan result. Physiotherapy can support movement and balance; occupational therapy can help with dressing, hand skills and everyday activities. Speech and language therapy may address communication or swallowing. Hearing and eye specialists can assess changes that make learning or social interaction harder. The combination of services should follow the child’s actual difficulties and goals.

Some children need help with attention, memory, processing information or emotions. Neuropsychological assessment can guide school support, while psychology services can help the child and family adjust. Discuss a manageable return to education, rest needs and any communication or mobility accommodations with the care team and school. New learning demands may reveal problems that were not obvious earlier, so support may need to change as the child grows.

Follow-up and the longer-term outlook

No single recovery timetable or survival figure describes all childhood brain tumors. Outlook depends on the exact diagnosis, molecular features, location, spread, response and the child’s functioning. Some children recover with few ongoing difficulties; others need prolonged treatment or lasting support. Ask the team what is known for your child, what remains uncertain and how it will judge progress.

Follow-up checks for tumor changes and for effects of the illness or its treatment. Ask for a treatment summary and a survivorship or long-term care plan covering scans, specialist reviews and relevant health checks. Depending on treatment, needs can include growth and puberty, hormones, hearing, vision, learning and emotional health. Share the plan with future clinicians. Care does not necessarily end when active treatment stops, and new symptoms should still be assessed between planned visits.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Seek care based on the severity and progression of symptoms, rather than using a symptom checklist to decide whether a tumor is present.

Ask the specialist team what each test or treatment will change and how safety and developing brain function are being protected.

Keep written urgent-care instructions and a follow-up plan that includes rehabilitation, education and possible late effects.

How BeMama can help

A useful next step is to write down the child’s symptoms and questions, identify the team’s contact route, and ask who will explain the next result. The treatment plan should account for the child’s everyday abilities as well as the tumor.

When to seek help

Call emergency services for severe breathing problems, reduced responsiveness, sudden neurological loss or a seizure emergency. During cancer treatment, fever or signs of infection need immediate advice; follow the team’s emergency plan and seek emergency care if timely contact is not possible. This information cannot determine a child’s diagnosis or treatment.

Evidence notes updated: November 10, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Persistent or worsening neurological changes need assessment, but symptoms alone cannot diagnose a tumor.
  • Severe or sudden neurological symptoms, reduced responsiveness and serious breathing problems require emergency help.
  • MRI, biopsy and cerebrospinal-fluid testing answer different questions; the specialist team selects the tests that are useful and safe.
  • Observation, surgery, radiation and medicines have different roles depending on the child and the tumor.
  • Rehabilitation, school support and long-term follow-up are part of care, including after active treatment ends.

Frequently asked questions

What causes a brain tumor in a child?

Usually no clear cause is identified. Most affected children have no known risk factor. Some genetic predisposition conditions raise risk, but a tumor is not evidence that a parent did something wrong or that every family member is at risk.

Does radiation exposure mean my child will develop a tumor?

No. Previous radiation treatment to the head can raise later risk, but a risk factor is not a prediction. CT uses much lower doses and should be chosen when clinically justified. Do not refuse an urgent needed scan without discussing the benefits and alternatives with the treating clinician.

Do mobile phones or power lines cause childhood brain tumors?

A causal link has not been established. Phones and power lines are different from ionizing radiation used in X-rays. Research continues, and uncertainty should not be confused with proof that an exposure caused an individual child’s tumor.

At what age can a child be diagnosed?

Brain tumors can occur from infancy through adolescence. Different types are more common at different ages, but age alone cannot confirm or exclude a tumor. Concerning symptoms should be assessed at any age; there is no routine screening scan for every healthy child.

Does every child need a biopsy or lumbar puncture?

No. Tissue often helps establish a precise diagnosis, but the benefit and safety of a biopsy depend on the situation. Cerebrospinal-fluid sampling is used for selected questions and must be safe, including assessment for raised pressure inside the skull.

Why might doctors watch a tumor instead of treating it immediately?

For selected stable tumors, monitoring can avoid treatment harm while checking for growth or functional changes. The plan needs scheduled reviews and clear triggers for treatment. It does not mean families should ignore new symptoms.

Can a young child receive radiation therapy?

Sometimes. Specialists weigh the tumor’s risk against possible effects on development. Age influences that balance, and alternatives may be considered, but it is not a universal prohibition. Ask why the proposed timing and technique are appropriate for your child.

When can my child return to their usual activities?

There is no single timetable. The team considers treatment, neurological recovery, fatigue, infection risk and the demands of school or activity. Rehabilitation and education support can be adjusted over time; do not interpret a slower recovery as a failure by the child or family.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
